questions.question: In a signalling game where a sender of privately known type sends a message to a receiver, what is a pooling equilibrium?
options: A perfect Bayesian equilibrium in which each type sends a different message
A perfect Bayesian equilibrium in which every type sends the same message
Any profile in which the receiver takes the same action after every message
A Nash equilibrium in which all types earn the same payoff

questions.question: In a pooling equilibrium of a signalling game, every sender type sends the message $m^*$. What is the receiver's belief $\mu(\theta\mid m^*)$ about the type?
options: Probability $1$ on the type that benefits most from $m^*$
Any distribution, since pooling makes beliefs uninformative
Equal probability on every type, whatever the prior
The common prior $p(\theta)$, since $m^*$ reveals nothing

questions.question: In a pooling equilibrium on message $m^*$, what is the status of the receiver's beliefs after a message $m\ne m^*$?
options: Irrelevant to the equilibrium, as no type ever sends $m$
Required to equal the prior, exactly as after the message $m^*$
Required by Bayes' rule to put probability $1$ on the worst type
Part of the equilibrium, but not restricted by Bayes' rule

questions.question: To verify that pooling on a message $m^*$ is a perfect Bayesian equilibrium of a signalling game, which set of checks is complete?
options: Prior after $m^*$; receiver optimal after every message; no type prefers another message
Prior after $m^*$; receiver optimal after $m^*$; no type prefers another message
Receiver optimal after every message; beliefs after every message equal the prior
No type prefers another message; beliefs after unused messages follow Bayes' rule

questions.question: Pooling equilibria in signalling games are often supported by particular beliefs after unused messages. Which beliefs typically do this, and why?
options: Pessimistic ones: a deviation is read as the bad type, so it does not pay
Optimistic ones: a deviation is read as the good type, so all types stay put
Prior beliefs: deviations are uninformative, so no type gains
Beliefs from Bayes' rule, which make every deviation unprofitable

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=0$. What is the receiver's belief $\mu(0)=\mathbb{P}(H\mid m=0)$, and what does she do after $m=0$?
options: $\mu(0)=0.5$; she is indifferent
$\mu(0)=0$; she rejects
$\mu(0)=0.4$; she rejects
$\mu(0)=0.4$; she accepts

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=0$; the off-path belief is $\mu(1)=0.7$ and the receiver replies optimally. What would $H$ get by deviating to $m=1$?

A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=0$. What is the most that type $L$ could get by deviating to $m=1$, over all possible off-path beliefs $\mu(1)$?

A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Could both types sending $m=1$ be a pooling perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: Yes, if the receiver believes $m=0$ comes from $L$
Yes: both types are treated alike, as pooling requires
No: $L$ gets $-3$, below her payoff from $m=0$
No: Bayes' rule would force $\mu(1)=1$ after $m=1$

questions.question: The sender's type is $A$, $B$ or $C$ with prior probabilities $0.2$, $0.3$ and $0.5$. Accepting gives the receiver $2$ against $A$, $1$ against $B$ and $-3$ against $C$; rejecting gives $0$. If all three types send the same message, what is accepting worth to the receiver, and what does she do?
options: $0$; she is indifferent
$-0.8$; she rejects
$-3$; she rejects
$2$; she accepts

questions.question: Two sender types differ greatly, yet a pooling equilibrium exists in a signalling game. How is this possible?
options: Large type differences make the receiver ignore all messages
Pooling needs the types to have equal payoffs from each message
The receiver learns the type anyway from payoffs after the game
Given the replies to other messages, no type gains by deviating

questions.question: In a pooling equilibrium of a signalling game every type sends $m^*$. How does the receiver's action after $m^*$ compare with what she would do if she could observe no message at all?
options: It favours the sender more, since sending $m^*$ is a choice
It is the same: in both cases she best responds to the prior
It favours the sender less, as pessimistic beliefs support pooling
It depends on her beliefs after the unused messages

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Proposed: both types send $m=0$, off-path belief $\mu(1)=0.8$, and rejection after both messages. Which requirement fails?
options: Bayes' rule after $m=1$, which requires $\mu(1)=0.4$
The on-path belief, since $\mu(0)$ must exceed $\mu(1)$
The receiver's response: with $\mu(1)=0.8$ she must accept
No requirement fails, since no type deviates to $m=1$

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=0$, which is rejected. For which off-path beliefs $\mu(1)$, with an optimal reply to $m=1$, is this a PBE?

In a signalling game $m=0$ is free and $m=1$ costs type $H$ an amount $c_H=1$; the sender gets $2$ if the receiver accepts and $0$ if she rejects, minus her cost. Two PBEs exist: in one both types send $m=0$ and are rejected; in the other $H$ sends $m=1$ and is accepted, while $L$ sends $m=0$ and is rejected. How do the types' payoffs under pooling compare with the other PBE?
options: Both types gain under pooling, as nobody pays a cost
$H$ gains $1$ under pooling and $L$ is unchanged
Neither changes, since $m=1$ produces nothing
$H$ loses $1$ under pooling and $L$ is unchanged

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.6$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=1.5$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=1$, and the off-path belief is $\mu(0)=0$. Is this a pooling perfect Bayesian equilibrium?
options: Yes: $H$ gets $1$, $L$ gets $0.5$, both above $0$ from $m=0$
No: pooling on the costly message is never an equilibrium
No: $L$ pays $1.5$ for a message that reveals nothing
Yes, but only if $\mu(0)$ equals the prior $0.6$

questions.question: In a signalling game, the receiver's action after $m^*$ is a best response to the prior. Which condition is necessary and sufficient for pooling on $m^*$ with that action to be a PBE?
options: Every off-path belief, with optimal responses, makes every type prefer $m^*$
Some off-path beliefs, with optimal responses, make every type weakly prefer $m^*$
The prior belief after every unused message deters all types
Some off-path beliefs make the receiver's payoff higher than after $m^*$

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $p$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=1$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Compare pooling on $m=0$ with $H$ alone sending $m=1$ and getting $2-1=1$. Does $H$ always prefer the latter?
options: No: if $p>\tfrac{1}{2}$, pooling is accepted and gives $H$ $2>1$
Yes: being identified always pays for the type the receiver wants
Yes, unless the off-path belief after $m=1$ is $0$
No: $H$ never gains from being identified, as $m=1$ is wasteful

questions.question: A sender, type $H$ (prior $0.4$) or $L$, sends $m=0$ for free or $m=1$ at cost $c_H=2.5$ or $c_L=3$. The receiver sees only $m$ and accepts (gaining $1$ from $H$, $-1$ from $L$) or rejects ($0$). The sender gets $2$ if accepted, $0$ if rejected, minus her cost. Both types send $m=0$, which is rejected. For which off-path beliefs $\mu(1)\in[0,1]$, with an optimal reply to $m=1$, is this a PBE?
options: For $\mu(1)\le\tfrac{1}{2}$ only
For $\mu(1)\le0.4$ only
For no belief, since $H$ would reveal herself
For every $\mu(1)\in[0,1]$

questions.question: A sender is strong ($S$, prior $0.7$) or weak and sends $B$ or $Q$; $S$ gets $1$ extra from $B$, the weak type $1$ extra from $Q$, and each gets $2$ if not fought. The receiver fights iff $\mu(S)\le\frac{1}{2}$. Which beliefs $\mu(S\mid Q)$ support pooling on $B$?
options: $\mu(S\mid Q)\le\frac{1}{2}$
$\mu(S\mid Q)>\frac{1}{2}$
$\mu(S\mid Q)=0.7$, the prior
Any $\mu(S\mid Q)$, since $Q$ is never sent
